topic.title: Rate limiter — token bucket vs sliding window at scale
topic.concept: A rate limiter protects downstreams by rejecting excess requests early; the algorithm choice trades burst tolerance against precision, and the storage choice trades accuracy against latency.
points: Token bucket allows bursts up to bucket size at refill rate r; fixed window suffers 2x boundary bursts; sliding window log is exact but O(requests) memory.
Sliding window counter (weighted two windows) is the practical middle: ~1.5% error, O(1) memory.
Distributed: counters in Redis with a Lua script for atomic read-increment-expire — avoids the check-then-set race.
Reject with 429 + Retry-After header; return X-RateLimit-Remaining so clients can self-throttle.
Decide the key first: per-user, per-API-key, per-IP (NAT punishes shared IPs) — and what happens when Redis is down (fail-open vs fail-closed).
topic.angle: 'Design a rate limiter for a public API.' Strong answers pick an algorithm WITH a reason, make the distributed counter atomic, and state the fail-open/fail-closed decision explicitly — that last one separates seniors.
